title: Drone Grants for Schools (2026): Fund the Teacher Too
sub_heading: What changed in school funding, the new limits on buying DJI drones with grant money, and why programs that fund only equipment stall.
body_html:
In short: School drone programs in 2026 are funded by a patchwork: Perkins V for CTE, Title IV-A for STEM, FAA workforce grants, state programs such as Pennsylvania's PAsmart, and local sponsors. Two things changed in the past year. Federal education money became less predictable, and federal rules now restrict buying DJI and Autel drones with grant funds. The lesson from 40 years of education technology still holds: programs that fund only the device stall. Fund the teacher, the consumables, and year two.

Key takeaways

  • The money that exists: Perkins V ($1.44B nationally), Title IV-A ($1.38B), FAA Aviation Workforce Development Grants (about $13M a year for pilots and drone operators), state CTE and STEM grants, and small grants.
  • What's gone or uncertain: pandemic ESSER money has run out, Title IV-A was briefly held back in 2025, and the FY27 budget request proposes consolidating 17 programs.
  • Hardware rules changed: since December 22, 2025, federal funds can't be used to buy or operate drones from covered makers such as DJI and Autel.
  • The evidence says fund people: the best long-term study of a device-first program found no learning gains after ten years, and research on teacher coaching shows real effects on student achievement.
  • Budget the full cost (spares, batteries, seats, teacher onboarding, year-two consumables, evaluation) and plan for funding beyond the grant from the start.

Two drones for a class that needed four

This fall a high school teacher won a grant for a drone project: students would map where their township's stormwater goes. The grant came through, and it bought two drones. The teacher had asked for four. Nothing was wrong with the application. Grants are usually written around the equipment, and the things that make a class period actually work (enough aircraft for every team, batteries that last a full period, spares, and time to train the teacher) get cut first.

That gap is the most common way a school drone program stalls, and it's avoidable. Here's what's changed in funding this year, where the money is, and how to budget so the program still works in year two.

What changed in 2025–2026

  • ESSER is over. Pandemic relief funds had to be obligated by September 30, 2024, and the final spending deadline passed in March 2026. Many districts bought equipment with ESSER and now need another source for upkeep.
  • Federal formula funds wobbled. On July 1, 2025, about $6.8 billion in school funds, including Title IV-A, was held back for 25 days before release. The FY2027 budget request proposes folding Title IV-A and 16 other programs into a single $2 billion grant.
  • Perkins V held steady at about $1.44 billion for FY26, with day-to-day administration moved to the Department of Labor in 2025. FY27 is running on a continuing resolution through December 11, 2026.
  • Drone purchasing rules tightened. The American Security Drone Act's prohibition took effect December 22, 2025: federal grant or contract funds can't buy or operate drones from covered manufacturers. The same day, the FCC added foreign-produced drones and critical components to its Covered List, which blocks new equipment authorizations. Drones you already own can still fly. There's no Department of Education guidance yet on how the ban applies to K–12 Perkins or Title IV-A purchases, so treat it as a real constraint and ask your district.

The lesson from 40 years of classroom technology

Two well-known programs show what happens when funding stops at the device.

One Laptop per Child in Peru gave laptops to students in rural schools and was studied more rigorously than almost any education technology program. A randomized trial in 318 schools found no effect on math or language scores. A ten-year follow-up across 531 schools, published in 2025, found no effect on school completion or university enrollment. Teachers received some training but did not improve their digital skills and rarely used the laptops in class.

Britain's BBC Micro (1980s) is remembered as a success. The device came with a national TV series, books, and a government program that built teacher-training networks and paid teachers to write software. Even then, a 2012 retrospective found that results in schools varied with the quality of local teacher training, and the UK scheme was criticized at the time for paying for equipment but not for maintenance, software, and staff training.

The wider research agrees. A review of 60 causal studies found that teacher coaching improved instruction substantially and raised student achievement (Kraft, Blazar & Hogan, 2018). A 2020 review of education technology experiments found that giving students access to computers alone generally does not raise test scores. Yet fewer than 40% of districts spend federal teacher-training money on technology training (SETDA, 2025).

For a drone program, the takeaway is simple: the aircraft is the cheap part. A trained teacher who can run a 45-minute class with them is the expensive, essential part.

Budget the full cost, not the box

A grant application that covers only aircraft leaves the program short by spring. Include:

Budget lineWhy it belongs in the grant
Aircraft or build kitsThe visible part
Spares, propellers, and enough batteries for a full class periodWhat actually makes a class session work
Course seats (Part 107 and any build or design course)The content layer
Teacher onboarding and professional developmentThe bottleneck in every study above; many grant programs pair equipment with PD
Year-two consumablesSo year two doesn't stall
EvaluationFunders ask for it, and it makes the next grant easier

Before you write drone hardware into a federally funded budget, confirm the make and model is allowed under current federal rules.

Plan for after the grant

Grants start programs; local value keeps them going. A sustainable plan usually moves through stages:

  1. Year 1: seed grant. Perkins, Title IV-A where allowed, a state STEM or CTE grant, or an FAA workforce grant.
  2. Years 1–2: a civic or employer partner. A township, conservation district, or local employer brings a real question (mapping a stormwater problem, surveying tree canopy) and helps fund the class that answers it.
  3. Ongoing: community giving. Education foundations, DonorsChoose, and local events.
  4. Year 3 and on: a district budget line. A program that has shown results earns a place in the CTE budget.

Measure from day one

Funders increasingly want evidence. Track real numbers from the start: students enrolled, units completed, exam scores, aircraft built, and the projects students delivered. Report Part 107 outcomes as school-reported results. If you can, set up a simple before-and-after comparison; it makes the year-two application stronger.

Questions answered

Can Perkins V funds buy drones?

Perkins V can fund equipment for approved CTE programs, and drones can qualify when they're part of one. Since December 22, 2025, federal funds can't buy or operate drones from covered manufacturers such as DJI and Autel. Confirm the specific make and model with your district before purchase.

Can we still buy DJI drones for our school?

Drones you already own can still be flown. Buying new DJI or Autel aircraft with federal grant money is restricted, and new foreign-made models face FCC authorization limits. Local or private funds have fewer restrictions, but check district policy.

What does the FAA Aviation Workforce Development Grant fund?

Programs that prepare students for careers as aircraft pilots, including drone operators, or in aviation maintenance. Past drone-related awards have funded high school curricula and teacher training. Applications open annually.

How much of a grant should go to teacher training?

There's no fixed rule. Budget it as its own line rather than assuming it's free, and include follow-up support during the first semester, not just a one-day workshop.
